Accordingly hunters, since they do not dare to set dogs on the porcupine, take it by a certain stratagem, which the same Oppian professed he would describe in what follows, but, prevented by death, he did not keep his promise. Nor is there reason for anyone to think that these things are said on poetic authority, since all who have written on the nature of animals report the same. Thus the Philosopher, History, book 9, [col. 1041] chapter 39, mentions certain animals τὰ βάλλοντα ταῖς θριξὶν, οἷον αἱ ὕστριχες [ta ballonta tais thrixin, hoion hai hystriches], which shoot their hairs, like porcupines. And Pliny, book 8, chapter 35: The porcupine has longer quills, and, when it stretches its skin, they can be shot. It pierces the mouths of dogs pressing on it, and shoots a little farther off. Solinus also: Bristling on its back with spines (the porcupine), which, often loosened, it discharges by voluntary shooting, so as to wound attacking dogs with continual showers of quills. And Aelian, book 1, chapter 31: Τὰς ἄνωθεν τρίχας οἱονεὶ βέλη ἐκπέμπει, καὶ εὐστόχως βάλλει πολλάκις, τὰ νῶτα φρίξασα, καὶ ἐκεῖναί γε πηδῶσιν. ὥσπερ οὖν ἔκ τινος ἀφειμέναι νευρᾶς· [Tas anōthen trichas hoionei belē ekpempei, kai eustochōs ballei pollakis, ta nōta phrixasa, kai ekeinai ge pēdōsin. hōsper oun ek tinos apheimenai neuras] It sends forth its upper hairs like arrows, and often aims them straight as at a target, contracting its back as it bristles. And they leap out as if shot from a bowstring. The Scholiast on Aristophanes on the Peace, and from him Suidas: Ἔστι δὲ ὕστριξ [II, 461] θηρίον τρίχας ἔχον ὑὸς, ἂν ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι ἐπακοντίζει κατὰ τῶν διωκόντων· [Esti de hystrix thērion trichas echon hyos, an en tō diōkesthai epakontizei kata tōn diōkontōn] The porcupine is a wild beast bristling with swine's bristles (whence its name), which, when someone pursues it, it shoots out at its pursuers. Porta coeli p. 19 d: גם יש מין מחוירי הבר שיש להם שערות גסים כמו חצים וזה לסבת גסות העור, There is a species of wild swine whose hairs are thick like arrows, namely because of the thickness and hardness of the skin. Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter قنفذ [qunfudh] Kunphud, والجبلي هو الدلدل ذو الشوك السهمي [wa-l-jabalī huwa al-duldul dhū al-shawk al-sahmī] And the mountain one (kunphud) is the duldul (porcupine), which has arrow-like spines, that is, missiles. Damir in the chapter دلدل [duldul] Duldul: واذا راي ما يكرهه انقبض فيخرج منه شوك كالمسال يخرج من اصابه والشوك الذي علي ظهره بحو الذراع [wa-idhā rāy mā yakrahuhu inqabaḍa fa-yakhruju minhu shawk ka-l-masāl yakhruju min aṣābahu wa-l-shawk alladhī ʿalī ẓahrihi bḥw al-dhirāʿ] And when it sees anything hostile, it contracts itself. And spines like needles come out of it, by which those pressing on it are wounded. And the spines that are on its back are about a cubit long. Marco Polo, book 1, chapter 33, on Scassem, a city of Tartary: In that region there are many spiny swine (porcupines), which, when they are caught, often injure men and dogs with their spines. For the dogs, set on the swine by the hunters, so provoke and stir up those beasts that, running together (contracting) their backs, on which the spines rest, they shake them violently, and with a certain violence discharge the very quills and hurl them at the nearer men and dogs. Gesner: It strikes whomever it wishes with a sure and aimed blow, with a wound sometimes almost incurable, being narrow and deep, dangerous indeed if a nerve is pierced. So that Oppian not without reason sings,
Ὑστρίγγων οὔπω τι πέλει κατὰ δάσκιον ὕλην Ῥίγιον εἰσιδέειν, ὅτ' ἀργαλεώτερον ἄλλο, [Hystringōn oupō ti pelei kata daskion hylēn Rhigion eisideein, hot' argaleōteron allo]
Which Stephanus condensed thus in his Notes on Callimachus:
Nothing in the shady woods is more dreadful to behold than the porcupine.
